From Kwong Fuk to Wang Fuk: A home chosen with the utmost care

In February this year, the government announced a proposal to acquire the ownership of the seven blocks of Wang Fuk Court. In late June, it announced that Wang Chi House, which had escaped the fire, would also be included in the acquisition. The entire estate will be demolished in the future and rebuilt as public facilities. Officials also said the primary principle of the acquisition is to combine "compassion, reason and the law," with "compassion" coming first.

Compassion is an abstract concept, usually expressed through words and actions. After the disaster, Mrs. Tan passes by Wang Fuk Court every day to take photographs. Her affection for the Kwong Fuk and Wang Fuk communities dates back to her childhood. She grew up in Kwong Fuk Estate, and after marriage she looked for a new home elsewhere in Tai Po but found nothing suitable. Her husband, who loves the sea, boldly declared he wanted to buy a sea-view flat. To their surprise, the agent actually found a listing in Wang Fuk Court, just a stone's throw away.

Buy despite bank's low valuation; moved in on the tenth anniversary of the handover

Mr. Tan said buying a flat is about a feeling. When they viewed the flat late at night at 11pm, "once we walked into the lobby with air-conditioning, it already felt wonderful." Nearly every window of the unit faced the sea, the moonlight shimmering on Tolo Harbour, a gentle breeze rustling the trees, bringing a sense of peace. "The agent said someone else was coming to view it the next day. The owner said if we put down a deposit now, the flat is ours." Mr. Tan hurried downstairs to withdraw cash, and by 1am they had signed the provisional agreement with the owner.

It was 2007. Others said the unit was not worth more than a million dollars, and the bank's valuation was also low. Yet the Tans were captivated and determined to buy. Coinciding with the tenth anniversary of the handover, the Reunification Tower opposite the building was graced with a rare fireworks display. They excitedly invited friends and relatives to their yet-to-be-renovated new home to watch, and even took their wedding photos at the seaside park, full of hopes for the future.

Estate gardens reveal deep community bonds

After their son Oscar was born, the ties between the small family and the community grew even closer. Neighbours on the same floor would leave their wooden doors open, and children would run over to play when they heard Oscar come home. The estate has a garden called "Lok Tao Garden" for residents to grow plants. It is so popular that a ballot is needed to take turns using it. Mrs. Tan laughs that they get the benefits without lifting a finger, as enthusiastic neighbours often help water the plants and let them know when the vegetables are ready for harvest. "A neighbour called to ask, would I mind if I plant some kale at your plot? Of course I wouldn't mind!" Their son loved seeing the sunrise just as he left for school. After dinner the family would stroll to the park to let off steam, and on holidays they would cycle along the river and the sea — all treasured memories.

Looking out for each other with neighbours; believing "we can return home soon"

On the day of the fire, Mrs. Tan and a neighbour she knew rushed home from the office. The neighbour's mother was trapped in the fire, and they were frantic with worry. They could only rush into the cordon to ask about the situation, and then there was nothing else they could do. Mrs. Tan turned to constantly contacting neighbours to check on their safety, reporting the number of people in each household to police officers, and reconfirming every hour. "It was chaotic — everything was just handwritten on A4 paper. I even asked the police if they could open an additional queue to help. It's just writing things down, but they had to find a caring team before opening another queue."

In the days that followed, the Tans accompanied a friend back and forth to the community hall, searching for news of the friend's mother. They directed members of the public who had spontaneously brought supplies to the scene and helped distribute them. "Mentally I couldn't go back to work, but we hadn't lost everything." Mr. Tan said the priority at that moment was "to comfort each other first, to look out for each other first." Both of them firmly believed they would be able to return home soon.

Questions hanging in the air; estimating that Wang Chi House alone could accommodate owners who have not yet sold

Yet their hopes were dashed time and again. They thought Wang Chi House had not been damaged and that residents would be free to come and go. "Who would have thought that by the time we were allowed back upstairs, it was already May? This really shouldn't be happening in Hong Kong." Initially, the government's questionnaire mentioned options including rebuilding on the original site or at the park opposite. They thought there was hope for the original site, but just two months after the fire the government announced there would be no rebuilding. They also thought at least Wang Chi House could remain, but in the end everyone was urged to sell their ownership and bid farewell to Wang Fuk Court for good.

Amid disappointment, questions also piled up. Un Chau Tsai Lane next to Wang Chi House was undamaged, and Mrs. Tan could not understand why they are still not allowed to go home the same way now: "Why restrict us from returning to a building that is perfectly fine?" Mr. Tan pointed out that the government had earlier said leaving Wang Chi House on its own would create legal issues such as maintenance costs, the sharing of management fees and the restructuring of deeds, but now that the government has become the major owner, the negotiations should be straightforward. Based on the figures released by the government, he estimates about 10% of owners are unwilling to sell, and the 248 flats in Wang Chi House would be just enough to house them.

"I cannot think of any reason to give up at the moment" — the government's 31 August acquisition deadline is imminent, and more than 90% of owners have already accepted the acquisition. Deputy Financial Secretary Wong Wai-lun stated that if legislation is required for the government to acquire ownership, property values would inevitably drop significantly. Everyone around them says "it will have to be acquired eventually," but the Tans have still not signed the letter accepting the acquisition offer. "I cannot think of any reason to give up at the moment." Mrs. Tan has been receiving constant reminder text messages from explainers lately and admits the pressure is mounting. Yet what weighs on her mind is not just her own property, but the entire Kwong Fuk and Wang Fuk community.

"From day one, what you have been doing is destroying the future of Kwong Fuk Estate. This insistence, apart from the fact that we truly love our home, is also about protecting the neighbours who are waiting for justice... we are putting in a little effort to protect Wang Fuk Court, and also the answers that everyone is truly waiting for. If everyone gives up so easily, this matter should have been resolved very quickly."

Repairs could save HK$900 million; urge wise use of public funds for Hong Kong

Taking an even broader view, she points out that acquiring Wang Chi House would cost HK$1 billion, whereas choosing to repair it could save at least HK$900 million of public funds. "Take that HK$900 million and put it into building Hong Kong's future, into education. Children are Hong Kong's future. I don't want you to spend HK$900 million demolishing a building that is safe to live in."
